doc.title: Al Gafa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2023

chapter: Playboy Club and the working life
title: Playboy Club band changes, a too-strong group, and five-night schedule
summary: Personnel changed after Monty left for Jilly's; the group drew crowds, and he worked studios by day and the club at night.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. Just a little bit more about this Playboy Club gig, did you get people coming up and asking for requests and sort of play them on the spot or did you pretty much get left alone?

No we got — okay so the Playboy was with Monty and Bob, there were hardly requests. Because these guys are monster musicians. You want to hear the guy play, you don’t want to pigeon hole him into one little song that your daughter likes or something like that. Yeah. I don’t remember requests coming in. But let me tell you what happened at this Playboy Club. After about maybe eight months or so Bob — I’m sorry Monty got a call for a job at Jilly’s and that was a nightclub in Manhattan that Sinatra used to hang out in and it was a noteworthy club to be in. So Monty left and the group changed. We brought in Larry Willis on piano, Earl May on drums, and the drummer at that time was Dick Berk.

Yeah. On that job he played electric bass, left handed electric bass. And so Dick Berk was with us and then after a while Dick left and we got Al Foster came in on drums. This group was dynamite. It was too strong for that club, and I’ll tell you what I mean. It was the first exposure to music that anybody walking in the club was exposed to this group. This group was so powerful that they did not want to go to any of the other rooms. They had showrooms, they had a dinner room, they had two rooms upstairs that had shows. And they had a dining room that had a trio. The group was so strong that people would just stay here. And it was worth it, it was just fun. And when we got to work over there we would be bashing from the first note to the end of the job. It was just fun. Nobody
wanted to stop playing. It was just, it was the epitome of having a good time playing music. It was just a monster.
Did the management notice that you were keeping people in this one spot and like you’re too good?

They never said you’re too good to us, but they, I’m sure they noticed that people, there was a stairway that they had to walk up to get to the elevators and the stairway was always crowded with people just stopping and listening. And then after, after they’d go, some of them would go to the shows, come down and sit at the piano bar that we were in. It worked out good for everybody.
And how many nights a week did you do this?

Five nights a week. Yeah. But this was during the time when I was working in the studios in the daytime like Monday through Friday, and the Playboy Club Tuesday through Saturday. So any money that I made I did not have a chance to spend it because I was working. Sometimes I’d have the guitar in my hand 12 hours, 16 hours a day, with the studio work and the stuff at night. I had no chance to spend it. It was a chance to bankroll some money at an early part in my career. It was really helpful.
